title: provide() / inject(): Dependency Injection & Readonly Reactive Wrappers

progressiveExplaining.eli5: If a great-grandparent wants to give a family heirloom to a great-grandchild, they don't have to pass it through every parent and child in the middle. The ancestor puts it in a family vault (`provide`), and any descendant can open the vault (`inject`) with a secret key. And to make sure the kids don't break the heirloom, the ancestor can lock it in view-only mode (`readonly`).
progressiveExplaining.junior: `provide(key, value)` allows an ancestor component to share data with all its descendants without prop drilling. Any child component calls `inject(key, defaultValue)` to read the value. If you pass a `ref()` or `reactive()` object to `provide`, changes made in the parent remain reactive in the child. To prevent children from mutating the shared state directly, wrap it in `readonly(state)`.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, `provide`/`inject` implements hierarchical Inversion of Control (IoC) scoped to the component tree instance. Unlike global Pinia/Vuex stores (which are singletons), provided dependencies are instance-scoped: multiple instances of a component subtree can provide different configurations. To enforce unidirectional data flow, the provider should expose updater functions alongside `readonly()` state wrappers rather than allowing descendants to mutate injected refs directly.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: In `@vue/runtime-core`, each `ComponentInternalInstance` has a `provides` object. By default, an instance inherits its parent's `provides` via `Object.create(parent.provides)`. When `provide(key, val)` is called, the component clones its `provides` object to shadow parent keys. When `inject(key)` is called, it performs an `O(1)` prototype chain lookup on `currentInstance.parent.provides[key]`. Injection keys using `Symbol()` provide compile-time TypeScript type safety via `InjectionKey<T>`.

codeComparison.title: Deep Prop Drilling vs provide/inject with readonly Protection
codeComparison.summary: Passing props through intermediate layers is fragile; `provide`/`inject` with `readonly` guarantees clean dependency injection.

fullFile.code:
<template>
  <!-- ❌ OLD: Intermediate components must accept and re-forward
       props they don't even use, cluttering component interfaces. -->
  <IntermediateLevelOne :theme="theme" :user="user" />
</template>

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue';
const theme = ref('dark');
const user = ref({ name: 'Ada' });
</script>

modernOrGood.label: provide/inject with readonly & Mutator
modernOrGood.snippet: provide('theme', { theme: readonly(theme), toggleTheme }); // ✅ NEW: Direct access with mutation safety

fullFile.code:
<script setup>
import { ref, readonly, provide } from 'vue';
import IntermediateLevelOne from './IntermediateLevelOne.vue';

const theme = ref('dark');

function toggleTheme() {
  theme.value = theme.value === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark';
}

// ✅ NEW: Provide readonly state + explicit updater method
provide('themeContext', {
  theme: readonly(theme),
  toggleTheme
});
</script>

<template>
  <IntermediateLevelOne />
</template>

interviewGotchas.question: Why should you pass `readonly()` wrapped refs to `provide()` in large applications?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your knowledge of unidirectional data flow and state architecture.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: If a raw mutable `ref` is provided, any deeply nested child component can mutate `theme.value = 'light'`, making it extremely difficult to track which component caused state bugs. Wrapping the ref in `readonly(theme)` and providing an explicit updater function (e.g. `toggleTheme`) ensures that state mutations remain owned and debuggable solely by the provider component.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Do not pass plain primitive values `provide('theme', theme.value)` if you want reactivity; pass the `ref` itself (or `readonly(ref)`).

interviewGotchas.question: How do you achieve TypeScript type safety with `provide` and `inject`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks TypeScript tooling expertise with Vue 3.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Use Vue's **`InjectionKey<T>`** utility with a `Symbol`: `export const ThemeKey: InjectionKey<Ref<string>> = Symbol('theme')`. When providing (`provide(ThemeKey, theme)`) and injecting (`const theme = inject(ThemeKey)`), TypeScript automatically infers the exact type `Ref<string>` without manual type casting.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Using raw string keys `provide('theme', ...)` loses TypeScript type inference and risks collisions across third-party plugins.
